analysis_note: All pre-1900 excerpts are plain-language renderings of public-domain sources.

documents.source_line: Letter from the Mongol imperial chancery (Güyük Khan) to Pope Innocent IV
documents.sourcing_note: Written by the Mongol court, addressed to the Pope; purpose is to assert universal Mongol dominion and demand submission. Shows both Mongol ideology of conquest and the existence of long-distance diplomatic communication.
documents.text_or_description: This is the command of Güyük Khan to the great Pope. You ask us to submit, but it is you who must come in person, with all your kings, to serve us. If you refuse our order, we will count you among our enemies. This is decreed by the power of the Eternal Heaven.

documents.source_line: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant, describing the court of the Great Khan (Khubilai)
documents.sourcing_note: A European merchant writing for a European audience; purpose is to describe the wealth and wonders he saw. His ability to travel from Venice to China and back illustrates the connectivity of the Mongol peace.
documents.text_or_description: In the city of Kanbalu the Great Khan has his mint. From the bark of mulberry trees they make a paper, cut into pieces of money of different values and stamped with the Khan's seal. All the people of his empire must accept it, and merchants from distant lands trade with it as readily as with gold.

documents.source_line: Francesco Pegolotti, Florentine merchant, in a handbook for traders (La Pratica della Mercatura)
documents.sourcing_note: A practical guide written by an Italian merchant for other merchants; purpose is commercial instruction, not praise. Its matter-of-fact tone about the safety of the route is strong evidence for routine, large-scale overland trade.
documents.text_or_description: The road from Tana to Cathay is safe to travel by day and by night. A merchant carrying goods can go with confidence, for the Tartars guard the route and punish robbers. Whatever a man spends on the journey, he will recover with profit in Cathay.

documents.source_line: William of Rubruck, Franciscan friar, reporting on the Mongol capital Karakorum
documents.sourcing_note: A Catholic missionary writing to King Louis IX of France; purpose is to report on prospects for conversion. His surprise at religious diversity reveals Mongol policy rather than his own agenda.
documents.text_or_description: In Karakorum I found Nestorian Christians with their churches, Muslims with their houses of prayer, and Buddhist monks with their temples. The Khan permits every faith to practice freely, and on appointed days their priests debate before him while he listens.

documents.source_line: The Novgorod Chronicle, written by Russian Orthodox monks
documents.sourcing_note: Written by monks of a city the Mongols did not destroy; audience is fellow Christians. Purpose is to lament the invasion as divine punishment. Its horror reflects the conquerors' violence, though the religious framing shapes the telling.
documents.text_or_description: In the winter the godless Tatars came against the land of Rus'. They surrounded the cities, burned the churches, and slew the people without mercy. There was weeping and wailing, and none remained to bury the dead.

documents.source_line: Animated map of Mongol Empire expansion, 1206-1294
documents.sourcing_note: A modern historian's animated map; purpose is to illustrate expansion and division. Supports both arguments: unprecedented political unification of Eurasia, achieved through conquest — and its later fragmentation.
documents.text_or_description: This animated map shows the Mongol Empire expanding from 1206 to 1294: a single empire stretching from Eastern Europe and Persia across Central Asia to China and Korea, ending divided into four khanates (Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate, Ilkhanate, Yuan).

documents.license: Public domain (14th-century album leaf; National Palace Museum, Taipei)
documents.source_line: Portrait of Genghis Khan from a Yuan dynasty imperial album
documents.sourcing_note: Painted by a Yuan court artist for the imperial court; purpose is dynastic legitimation. A Mongol conqueror portrayed in the formal style of Chinese imperial portraiture shows cultural synthesis at the top of the empire.
documents.text_or_description: A formal seated portrait of Genghis Khan in imperial robes, painted in the traditional Chinese court style generations after his death.

prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the extent to which Mongol rule promoted or hindered cultural and economic exchange across Eurasia in the period c. 1200-1400.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: argue exchange flourished because of conquest (Pax Mongolica) vs. despite it; corroborate trade claims across Docs 2 and 3; qualify by region (Doc 5 destruction in Rus' vs. Doc 4 tolerance at Karakorum); note Doc 1 itself is evidence of long-distance communication even as it threatens war.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (audience/purpose: a demand for submission sent across continents); Doc 3 (purpose: a merchant manual, unusually reliable on trade conditions); Doc 4 (point of view: a missionary surprised by tolerance); Doc 5 (context/purpose: monks framing invasion as divine punishment).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate Mongol expansion within the post-Abbasid fragmentation of Eurasia, the Song-Jin wars in China, and the growth of long-distance trade before 1200 (e.g., the Silk Roads under earlier empires).

evidence.describe: All seven documents are describable; strongest for describe-and-explain: Docs 2, 3, 4 (mechanisms of exchange), Doc 5 (destruction).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the Yam postal relay system; transfer of gunpowder, printing, and medical knowledge; the Black Death's spread along Mongol trade routes; destruction of Baghdad (1258) and its libraries.
evidence.support: 'Promoted' line: Docs 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. 'Hindered' line: Docs 1, 5. Doc 6 (map) serves both: unity enabling trade, unity built by conquest.

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'extent' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

sample_thesis: Although Mongol conquests brought terrible destruction to cities like those of Rus', Mongol rule promoted cultural and economic exchange across Eurasia to a greater extent because the Mongols' unification of the continent, religious tolerance, and protection of merchants created safer and more connected trade routes than had existed before.
title: The Mongols and Eurasian Exchange
